input.quote: 19.2 For ninety days after delivery or acceptance, whichever is later, each Deliverable will materially conform to its documentation and acceptance criteria. Hosted Services will conform throughout the subscription term. Vendor warrants it has authority to enter the Agreement and grant the rights stated here.
input.rationale:
WARRANTY PERIOD (addressing the failed deterministic check): Section 19.2 sets the Deliverable conformity period at "ninety days after delivery or acceptance, whichever is later." The period is spelled out in words rather than as the numeral "90", which is what caused the "period >= 90 days or expressed in months/years" check to fail; ninety days equals 90 days and therefore meets the preferred 90-day services/Deliverable benchmark exactly. The check failure is a false negative on formatting, not a substantive shortfall. Two features in fact exceed the benchmark: the clock runs from the LATER of delivery or acceptance rather than delivery alone, and Hosted Services must conform throughout the entire subscription term, which surpasses the 12-month software benchmark for the hosted scope. I have re-cited the quote to Section 19.2 (rather than the remedy in 19.4) so the period language is on the face of the evidence.

REMAINING ELEMENTS: Section 19.1 gives a professional and workmanlike services warranty by qualified personnel in accordance with industry standards, plus material conformity of Services and Deliverables to documentation and specifications. Section 19.3 covers no malicious code and compliance with Applicable Law, and adds no-functionality-diminishment and open-source protections. Section 19.4 supplies the full re-perform/repair/replace remedy with a termination-and-refund backstop and is expressly non-exclusive for fraud, infringement, confidentiality, privacy, security, and indemnified claims, so the "sole remedy" narrowing we resist is absent. Section 19.5 limits the disclaimer to implied warranties, is mutual, and expressly provides that no disclaimer limits an express warranty, service level, indemnity or remedy, so the disclaimer does not swallow the express warranty. No "AS IS" or sole-remedy language appears anywhere; Sections 3.1 and 6 reinforce rather than undercut the warranty.

NOTED BUT NOT FLAGGED: the malicious-code warranty in 19.3 is limited to code "intentionally introduced by Vendor", which is narrower than a flat "no malicious code" and would not reach malware negligently passed through in a third-party component. This is a common market formulation and, given the strong non-exclusive remedy and the security obligations carried as Excluded Claims under Section 21.3, it does not change the compliant characterization. Worth raising only if this negotiation reopens Section 19 for other reasons. No redline proposed.
